claim: EFA-6 is a potent intrinsic inhibitor of axon regrowth in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans the signaling protein Exchange Factor for ARF-6 (EFA-6) is a potent intrinsic inhibitor of axon regrowth.
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by references to prior work (Chen et al., 2011) cited in the introduction.

claim: Axon injury triggers rapid EFA-6-dependent inhibition of axonal microtubule dynamics.
source: Here we show that axon injury triggers rapid EFA-6-dependent inhibition of axonal microtubule (MT) dynamics, concomitant with relocalization of EFA-6.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: EFA-6 relocalizes after axon injury.
source: Here we show that axon injury triggers rapid EFA-6-dependent inhibition of axonal microtubule (MT) dynamics, concomitant with relocalization of EFA-6.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: EFA-6 relocalization and axon regrowth inhibition require a conserved 18-aa motif in its N-terminal domain.
source: EFA-6 relocalization and axon regrowth inhibition require a conserved 18-aa motif in its otherwise intrinsically disordered N-terminal domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 1 and 2, showing that deletion of the 18-aa motif abolishes relocalization and function.

claim: The EFA-6 N-terminus binds the MT-associated protein TAC-1/Transforming-Acidic-Coiled-Coil.
source: The EFA-6 N-terminus binds the MT-associated proteins TAC-1/Transforming-Acidic-Coiled-Coil, and ZYG-8/Doublecortin-Like-Kinase, both of which are required for regenerative growth cone formation, and which act downstream of EFA-6.
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid and co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The EFA-6 N-terminus binds ZYG-8/Doublecortin-Like-Kinase.
source: The EFA-6 N-terminus binds the MT-associated proteins TAC-1/Transforming-Acidic-Coiled-Coil, and ZYG-8/Doublecortin-Like-Kinase, both of which are required for regenerative growth cone formation, and which act downstream of EFA-6.
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid and co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: TAC-1 and ZYG-8 are required for regenerative growth cone formation.
source: The EFA-6 N-terminus binds the MT-associated proteins TAC-1/Transforming-Acidic-Coiled-Coil, and ZYG-8/Doublecortin-Like-Kinase, both of which are required for regenerative growth cone formation, and which act downstream of EFA-6.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing reduced growth cone formation in tac-1 and zyg-8 mutants.

claim: TAC-1 and ZYG-8 act downstream of EFA-6.
source: The EFA-6 N-terminus binds the MT-associated proteins TAC-1/Transforming-Acidic-Coiled-Coil, and ZYG-8/Doublecortin-Like-Kinase, both of which are required for regenerative growth cone formation, and which act downstream of EFA-6.
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: After injury, TAC-1 and EFA-6 transiently relocalize to sites marked by the MT minus end binding protein PTRN-1/Patronin.
source: After injury TAC-1 and EFA-6 transiently relocalize to sites marked by the MT minus end binding protein PTRN-1/Patronin.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization imaging data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: EFA-6 acts as a bifunctional injury-responsive regulator of axonal MT dynamics, acting at the cell cortex in the steady state and at MT minus ends after injury.
source: We propose that EFA-6 acts as a bifunctional injury-responsive regulator of axonal MT dynamics, acting at the cell cortex in the steady state and at MT minus ends after injury.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: The mammalian CNS expresses myelin-associated proteins that inhibit regeneration.
source: The mammalian central nervous system (CNS) expresses a variety of environmental regeneration inhibitory factors, including myelin-associated proteins, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and glial scar tissue that functions as a physical barrier (Schwab, 2004; Silver and Miller, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Schwab, 2004; Silver and Miller, 2004).

claim: The mammalian CNS expresses chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans that inhibit regeneration.
source: The mammalian central nervous system (CNS) expresses a variety of environmental regeneration inhibitory factors, including myelin-associated proteins, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and glial scar tissue that functions as a physical barrier (Schwab, 2004; Silver and Miller, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Schwab, 2004; Silver and Miller, 2004).

claim: Glial scar tissue functions as a physical barrier to axon regeneration in the mammalian CNS.
source: The mammalian central nervous system (CNS) expresses a variety of environmental regeneration inhibitory factors, including myelin-associated proteins, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and glial scar tissue that functions as a physical barrier (Schwab, 2004; Silver and Miller, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Schwab, 2004; Silver and Miller, 2004).

claim: Genetic removal of environmental inhibitory factors results in only limited improvement in regeneration of severed axons.
source: However genetic removal of these inhibitory factors results in only limited improvement in regeneration of severed axons (Lee et al., 2009, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Lee et al., 2009, 2010).

claim: Loss of function in PTEN can dramatically improve axon regrowth in the inhibitory CNS environment.
source: Loss of function in cell-intrinsic growth inhibitors such as Phosphatase and Tensin homolog, PTEN, and Suppressor Of Cytokine Signaling-3, SOCS3, can dramatically improve axon regrowth even in the inhibitory CNS environment (Park et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Park et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2011).

claim: Loss of function in SOCS3 can dramatically improve axon regrowth in the inhibitory CNS environment.
source: Loss of function in cell-intrinsic growth inhibitors such as Phosphatase and Tensin homolog, PTEN, and Suppressor Of Cytokine Signaling-3, SOCS3, can dramatically improve axon regrowth even in the inhibitory CNS environment (Park et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Park et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2011).

claim: Axonal growth cones are enriched in dynamic MTs.
source: Cellular compartments undergoing rapid morphological changes, such as axonal growth cones, are enriched in dynamic MTs (Suter et al., 2004), while mature axons or dendrites contain predominantly stabilized MTs (Baas et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Suter et al., 2004).

claim: Mature axons or dendrites contain predominantly stabilized MTs.
source: Cellular compartments undergoing rapid morphological changes, such as axonal growth cones, are enriched in dynamic MTs (Suter et al., 2004), while mature axons or dendrites contain predominantly stabilized MTs (Baas et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Baas et al., 1993).

claim: When an axon is injured, MTs are locally disassembled or severed.
source: When an axon is injured, MTs are locally disassembled or severed, potentially creating free plus ends for new MT polymerization.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of MT responses to injury.

claim: Moderate stabilization of MT dynamics by Taxol can promote axon regrowth in vitro and in the mammalian CNS.
source: Moderate stabilization of MT dynamics by Taxol or other MT stabilizers can promote axon regrowth in vitro and in the mammalian CNS (Usher et al., 2010; Hellal et al., 2011; Sengottuvel et al., 2011; Ruschel et al., 2015); the effects of Taxol in vivo have been partly replicated (Popovich et al., 2014; Ruschel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Usher et al., 2010; Hellal et al., 2011; Sengottuvel et al., 2011; Ruschel et al., 2015).

claim: EFA-6 was identified as an intrinsic inhibitor of axon regrowth in a large-scale screen in C. elegans.
source: In a large-scale screen for genes affecting adult axon regeneration in Caenorhabditis elegans, we identified Exchange Factor for ARF-6 (EFA-6) as an intrinsic inhibitor of axon regrowth (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: The EFA-6/EFA6 protein family is conserved from yeast to mammals.
source: The EFA-6/EFA6 protein family is conserved from yeast to mammals, and is defined by its Sec7 domain, which confers guanine exchange factor (GEF) activity for Arf6 GTPases (Franco et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Franco et al., 1999).

claim: The Sec7 domain of EFA-6 confers guanine exchange factor (GEF) activity for Arf6 GTPases.
source: The EFA-6/EFA6 protein family is conserved from yeast to mammals, and is defined by its Sec7 domain, which confers guanine exchange factor (GEF) activity for Arf6 GTPases (Franco et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Franco et al., 1999).

claim: The regrowth-inhibitory function of EFA-6 is independent of its GEF activity.
source: Unexpectedly, the regrowth-inhibitory function of EFA-6 is independent of its GEF activity, and instead is mediated by its N-terminal domain (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: The regrowth-inhibitory function of EFA-6 is mediated by its N-terminal domain.
source: Unexpectedly, the regrowth-inhibitory function of EFA-6 is independent of its GEF activity, and instead is mediated by its N-terminal domain (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: The EFA-6 N-terminal domain inhibits MT growth at the cell cortex of C. elegans embryos via a conserved motif of 18 amino acids.
source: The EFA-6 N-terminal domain inhibits MT growth at the cell cortex of C. elegans embryos via a conserved motif of 18 amino acids (O'Rourke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (O'Rourke et al., 2010).

claim: Full-length EFA-6 tagged with GFP at the N- or C-termini localized to the plasma membrane of the soma and processes of neurons.
source: Full-length EFA-6 tagged with GFP at the N- or C-termini, expressed at a range of concentrations, localized to the plasma membrane of the soma and processes of neurons (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Deletion of the PH domain from EFA-6 results in cytosolic localization.
source: deletion of the PH domain (FLΔPH) resulted in cytosolic localization (Figure 1C, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The first 150 residues of the EFA-6 N-terminus (N150) localized to the cytosol.
source: The first 150 residues of the EFA-6 N-terminus (N150), expression of which inhibits axon regrowth (Chen et al., 2011), was localized to the cytosol similarly to FLΔPH (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: EFA-6 proteins lacking the N-terminal 150 amino acids (FLΔN150) showed plasma membrane localization resembling that of full-length EFA-6.
source: Conversely, EFA-6 proteins lacking the N-terminal 150 amino acids (FLΔN150) showed plasma membrane localization resembling that of full-length EFA-6 (Figure 1B,E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B,E.

claim: Within seconds of laser axotomy of the PLM axon, GFP::EFA-6FL redistributed from a generally even plasma membrane localization to more discrete puncta.
source: Within seconds of laser axotomy of the PLM axon, GFP::EFA-6FL redistributed from a generally even plasma membrane localization to more discrete puncta (Figure 1B, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: EFA-6 relocalization after injury does not require the PH domain.
source: This relocalization was also observed when GFP was tagged to the C terminus or in the middle of EFA-6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and did not require the PH domain (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GFP::EFA-6N150 became punctate after injury.
source: GFP::EFA-6N150, although not membrane associated, also became punctate after injury, whereas GFP::EFA-6FLΔN150 did not relocalize after axon injury (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GFP::EFA-6FLΔN150 did not relocalize after axon injury.
source: GFP::EFA-6N150, although not membrane associated, also became punctate after injury, whereas GFP::EFA-6FLΔN150 did not relocalize after axon injury (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Full-length EFA-6 and the N terminal domain (N150) relocalize to the same puncta in response to injury.
source: Full-length EFA-6 and the N terminal domain (N150) appear to relocalize to the same puncta in response to injury, as shown by co-expressing EFA-6FL::GFP and EFA-6N150::mKate2 (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization imaging data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The region of relocalized EFA-6FL or EFA-6N150 expanded bidirectionally from the injury site at ∼8 μm s−1.
source: The region of relocalized EFA-6FL or EFA-6N150 expanded bidirectionally from the injury site at ∼8 μm s−1, into the soma and dendrite (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and Video 1.

claim: The density of injury-triggered puncta of EFA-6FL and EFA-6N150 gradually decreased over the next 20–60 min.
source: The density of injury-triggered puncta of EFA-6FL and EFA-6N150 gradually decreased over the next 20–60 min (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: Injury-triggered EFA-6 relocalization occurs in multiple neuron types, irrespective of the site of injury.
source: We observed similar re-localization of GFP::EFA-6 after injury of motor neuron axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E), as well as when injury was delivered to the soma, distal axon, or posterior processes of mechanosensory neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F). These results indicate that injury-triggered EFA-6 relocalization occurs in multiple neuron types, irrespective of the site of injury and independent of the Sec7 or PH domains.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E,F.

claim: Injury-triggered EFA-6 relocalization is independent of the Sec7 or PH domains.
source: These results indicate that injury-triggered EFA-6 relocalization occurs in multiple neuron types, irrespective of the site of injury and independent of the Sec7 or PH domains.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that EFA-6 fragments lacking these domains still relocalize after injury.

claim: The N-terminal 1–70 aa (N70) was the smallest fragment tested that displayed relocalization after injury.
source: The N-terminal 1–70 aa (N70) was the smallest fragment tested that displayed relocalization after injury (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In uninjured neurons, EFA-6FL::GFP recovered with t½ = 4 s and an immobile fraction of 25% in FRAP experiments.
source: In uninjured neurons, EFA-6FL::GFP recovered with t½ = 4 s and an immobile fraction of 25%.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: EFA-6FL::GFP puncta 2 min after injury showed dramatically reduced recovery, with >85% of the protein in the immobile fraction.
source: In contrast, EFA-6FL::GFP puncta 2 min after injury showed dramatically reduced recovery, with >85% of the protein in the immobile fraction (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: By 1 hr after injury, EFA-6FL::GFP partially returned to its steady state localization.
source: By 1 hr after injury, EFA-6FL::GFP partially returned to its steady state localization (Figure 1B), and its recovery rate was partially restored, with an immobile fraction of 50% (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and FRAP data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 2A,B.

claim: After injury EFA-6 is sequestered to subcellular structures.
source: This analysis suggests that after injury EFA-6 is sequestered to subcellular structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP data showing reduced mobility after injury.

claim: efa-6(lf) mutants display significantly increased PLM axon regrowth following laser axotomy in adults.
source: efa-6(lf) mutants display significantly increased PLM axon regrowth following laser axotomy in adults, as well as impenetrant developmental overshooting of PLM axons; conversely, overexpression of EFA-6 strongly inhibits axon regrowth after axotomy, and causes premature truncation of PLM axon growth ('undershooting') in development (Chen et al., 2011) (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D and citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: efa-6(lf) mutants display impenetrant developmental overshooting of PLM axons.
source: efa-6(lf) mutants display significantly increased PLM axon regrowth following laser axotomy in adults, as well as impenetrant developmental overshooting of PLM axons; conversely, overexpression of EFA-6 strongly inhibits axon regrowth after axotomy, and causes premature truncation of PLM axon growth ('undershooting') in development (Chen et al., 2011) (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: Overexpression of EFA-6 strongly inhibits axon regrowth after axotomy.
source: efa-6(lf) mutants display significantly increased PLM axon regrowth following laser axotomy in adults, as well as impenetrant developmental overshooting of PLM axons; conversely, overexpression of EFA-6 strongly inhibits axon regrowth after axotomy, and causes premature truncation of PLM axon growth ('undershooting') in development (Chen et al., 2011) (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: Overexpression of EFA-6 causes premature truncation of PLM axon growth ('undershooting') in development.
source: efa-6(lf) mutants display significantly increased PLM axon regrowth following laser axotomy in adults, as well as impenetrant developmental overshooting of PLM axons; conversely, overexpression of EFA-6 strongly inhibits axon regrowth after axotomy, and causes premature truncation of PLM axon growth ('undershooting') in development (Chen et al., 2011) (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: Overexpression of the EFA-6 N terminal fragments N150, N100, N70 caused axons of PLM neurons to undershoot.
source: We found that overexpression of the EFA-6 N terminal fragments that displayed injury-induced relocalization (N150, N100, N70) all caused axons of PLM neurons to undershoot (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and Table 1.

claim: Overexpression of smaller fragments (N24, N42 or N[43–70 aa]) of the EFA-6 N-terminus did not significantly inhibit PLM outgrowth or regrowth.
source: In contrast, overexpression of smaller fragments (N24, N42 or N[43–70 aa]) of the EFA-6 N-terminus that did not relocalize in response to axotomy did not significantly inhibit PLM outgrowth or regrowth (Figure 2C,D and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D and Table 1.

claim: Overexpression of EFA-6FLΔN150 caused PLM overshooting.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of EFA-6FLΔN150, but not of EFA-6FL, caused PLM overshooting, suggesting the C-terminal region of EFA-6 may inhibit the activity of the N-terminus.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: The C-terminal region of EFA-6 may inhibit the activity of the N-terminus.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of EFA-6FLΔN150, but not of EFA-6FL, caused PLM overshooting, suggesting the C-terminal region of EFA-6 may inhibit the activity of the N-terminus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that overexpression of EFA-6FLΔN150 causes overshooting while full-length EFA-6 does not.

claim: Overexpression of EFA-6FL strongly inhibits axonal MT dynamics.
source: Overexpression of EFA-6FL strongly inhibits axonal MT dynamics, as assessed using the EBP-GFP assay for growing MT plus ends (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: Only those EFA-6 fragments displaying injury-induced relocalization also inhibited steady-state axonal MT dynamics when overexpressed.
source: Using live imaging and quantitative kymograph analysis of EBP-2::GFP comets, we found that only those EFA-6 fragments displaying injury-induced relocalization also inhibited steady-state axonal MT dynamics when overexpressed (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The ability of EFA-6 protein fragments to inhibit axon growth and MT dynamics closely correlates with their ability to relocalize in response to injury.
source: These observations suggest the ability of EFA-6 protein fragments to inhibit axon growth and MT dynamics closely correlates with their ability to relocalize in response to injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation observed between relocalization and functional effects.

claim: The 18 aa motif is necessary for EFA-6's effects on cortical MT growth in the embryo.
source: All EFA6 family members contain extended N-termini of low sequence complexity and lack defined sequence motifs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). The sole known region of sequence conservation among N-termini of some EFA6 family members is a motif of 18 aa (residues 25–42 in C. elegans EFA-6), necessary and partially sufficient for EFA-6's effects on cortical MT growth in the embryo (O'Rourke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (O'Rourke et al., 2010).

claim: The EFA-6 N-terminus has a high probability of protein disorder, with the exception of the 18 aa motif.
source: Analysis of EFA-6/EFA6 N-termini using algorithms that predict natively disordered protein regions (Xue et al., 2010) indicates that the EFA-6 N-terminus has a high probability of protein disorder, with the exception of the 18 aa motif (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and citation to the prediction method (Xue et al., 2010).

claim: Full length EFA-6 lacking the 18 aa motif (GFP::EFA-6FLΔ18) localized to the plasma membrane but did not cause axonal developmental defects.
source: We found that full length EFA-6 lacking the motif, GFP::EFA-6FLΔ18, localized to the plasma membrane but did not cause axonal developmental defects (Figures 1G, 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1G and 2C.

claim: Deletion of the 18 aa motif from the N-terminus (N150Δ18) abolished nuclear exclusion of GFP::EFA-6N150.
source: GFP::EFA-6N150 was diffuse in the cytosol and excluded from the nucleus (Figure 1D). Deletion of the 18 aa motif from the N-terminus (N150Δ18) abolished this nuclear exclusion, largely resembling free GFP (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 1D and 1H.

claim: Overexpression of EFA-6N150Δ18 did not cause developmental abnormalities.
source: Overexpression of EFA-6N150Δ18 also did not cause developmental abnormalities (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pan-neural overexpression of EFA-6N150 caused aberrant locomotion.
source: Pan-neural overexpression of EFA-6N150, but not of EFA-6N150Δ18, caused aberrant locomotion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E), suggesting that high levels of EFA-6 N-terminal domain perturb function of many neurons, in a manner dependent on the 18 aa motif.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Pan-neural overexpression of EFA-6N150Δ18 did not cause aberrant locomotion.
source: Pan-neural overexpression of EFA-6N150, but not of EFA-6N150Δ18, caused aberrant locomotion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E), suggesting that high levels of EFA-6 N-terminal domain perturb function of many neurons, in a manner dependent on the 18 aa motif.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Mutating 2 or more residues within the 18 aa motif to alanines significantly reduced the activity of the N-terminus in multiple assays.
source: Moreover, mutating 2 or more residues within the 18 aa motif to alanines significantly reduced the activity of the N-terminus in multiple assays (Table 1), suggesting the sequence of the 18 aa motif is critical for the N-terminus to function.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: The 18 aa motif was essential for injury-triggered relocalization of EFA-6FL and EFA-6N150.
source: The 18 aa motif was essential for injury-triggered relocalization of EFA-6FL and EFA-6N150 (Figure 1G,H), as well as for their inhibitory effects in axon regrowth (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1G,H and 2D.

claim: The 18 aa motif was essential for the inhibitory effects of EFA-6FL and EFA-6N150 in axon regrowth.
source: The 18 aa motif was essential for injury-triggered relocalization of EFA-6FL and EFA-6N150 (Figure 1G,H), as well as for their inhibitory effects in axon regrowth (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Expression of the 18 aa motif alone did not cause PLM developmental defects or confer injury-induced re-localization.
source: Expression of the 18 aa motif alone did not cause PLM developmental defects or confer injury-induced re-localization (Figures 1I, 2C), but mildly inhibited axon regrowth (Figure 2D), suggesting that injured axons are highly sensitive to the activity of this motif, but that the surrounding context is required for full activity of the N terminus.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1I, 2C, and 2D.

claim: Expression of the 18 aa motif alone mildly inhibited axon regrowth.
source: Expression of the 18 aa motif alone did not cause PLM developmental defects or confer injury-induced re-localization (Figures 1I, 2C), but mildly inhibited axon regrowth (Figure 2D), suggesting that injured axons are highly sensitive to the activity of this motif, but that the surrounding context is required for full activity of the N terminus.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: efa-6(tm3124) and efa-6(ok3353) delete genomic sequences that encode the Sec7 domain.
source: Two efa-6 loss of function alleles, tm3124 and ok3353, delete genomic sequences that encode the Sec7 domain, and are predicted to cause frameshifts after the N-terminus (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the genomic structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: efa-6(tm3124) and efa-6(ok3353) cause embryonic phenotypes similar to efa-6 RNAi.
source: Both mutations cause embryonic phenotypes similar to efa-6 RNAi (O'Rourke et al., 2010) and display similarly enhanced axon regrowth (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (O'Rourke et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2011).

claim: efa-6(tm3124) and efa-6(ok3353) display similarly enhanced axon regrowth.
source: Both mutations cause embryonic phenotypes similar to efa-6 RNAi (O'Rourke et al., 2010) and display similarly enhanced axon regrowth (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: efa-6(ju1200) removes the genomic sequences encoding the 18 aa motif.
source: We therefore generated a targeted deletion, efa-6(ju1200), that removes the genomic sequences encoding the 18 aa motif (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the genomic structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The axon developmental and regrowth phenotypes of efa-6(ju1200) mutants were indistinguishable from those of efa-6(tm3124).
source: The axon developmental and regrowth phenotypes of efa-6(ju1200) mutants were indistinguishable from those of efa-6(tm3124) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Single copy transgene expression of EFA-6N150 (juSi86) rescued the regeneration defects of both efa-6(tm3124) and efa-6(ju1200) to similar degrees.
source: In addition, single copy transgene expression of EFA-6N150 (juSi86) rescued the regeneration defects of both efa-6(tm3124) and efa-6(ju1200) to similar degrees (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), and also rescued developmental axon overgrowth (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The increased axon regrowth of efa-6 mutants reflects a complete loss of EFA-6 function.
source: Thus, the increased axon regrowth of efa-6 mutants reflects a complete loss of EFA-6 function, and the major activity of EFA-6 in axon growth resides in the N-terminus, dependent on the 18 aa motif.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and rescue experiments.

claim: The major activity of EFA-6 in axon growth resides in the N-terminus, dependent on the 18 aa motif.
source: Thus, the increased axon regrowth of efa-6 mutants reflects a complete loss of EFA-6 function, and the major activity of EFA-6 in axon growth resides in the N-terminus, dependent on the 18 aa motif.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and rescue experiments.

claim: TAC-1 and ZYG-8 were identified as strong interactors of the EFA-6 N-terminus in yeast two-hybrid screening.
source: To understand how EFA-6 inhibits axon regeneration, we next searched for EFA-6 interacting proteins using yeast two-hybrid screening. We identified two strong interactors, the MT-associated proteins (MAPs) TAC-1 and ZYG-8.
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ZYG-8 is the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian DCLK.
source: ZYG-8 is the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian DCLK, defined by an N-terminal doublecortin domain and a C-terminal kinase domain (Gönczy et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gönczy et al., 2001).

claim: ZYG-8 is required for spindle positioning in embryos.
source: ZYG-8 is required for spindle positioning in embryos (Gönczy et al., 2001), and for normal axonal MT architecture in post-mitotic neurons (Bellanger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gönczy et al., 2001).

claim: ZYG-8 is required for normal axonal MT architecture in post-mitotic neurons.
source: ZYG-8 is required for spindle positioning in embryos (Gönczy et al., 2001), and for normal axonal MT architecture in post-mitotic neurons (Bellanger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Bellanger et al., 2012).

claim: TAC-1 is the sole TACC protein in C. elegans.
source: TAC-1 is the sole TACC protein in C. elegans (Bellanger and Gönczy, 2003; Le Bot et al., 2003; Srayko et al., 2003) and can form a complex with ZYG-8 to regulate MT assembly in embryos (Bellanger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Bellanger and Gönczy, 2003; Le Bot et al., 2003; Srayko et al., 2003).

claim: TAC-1 can form a complex with ZYG-8 to regulate MT assembly in embryos.
source: TAC-1 is the sole TACC protein in C. elegans (Bellanger and Gönczy, 2003; Le Bot et al., 2003; Srayko et al., 2003) and can form a complex with ZYG-8 to regulate MT assembly in embryos (Bellanger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Bellanger et al., 2007).

claim: Both TAC-1 and ZYG-8 interacted with EFA-6N150 in the yeast two-hybrid assay, dependent on the 18 aa motif.
source: In the yeast two-hybrid assay, we found that both TAC-1 and ZYG-8 interacted with EFA-6N150, dependent on the 18 aa motif (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAC-1 and ZYG-8 interacted by two-hybrid assay.
source: TAC-1 and ZYG-8 interacted by two-hybrid assay, and TAC-1 interacted strongly with ZYG-8ΔKD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAC-1 interacted strongly with ZYG-8ΔKD in the two-hybrid assay.
source: TAC-1 and ZYG-8 interacted by two-hybrid assay, and TAC-1 interacted strongly with ZYG-8ΔKD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAC-1 co-immunoprecipitated with EFA-6N150, but not with EFA-6N150Δ18.
source: To independently verify these interactions we transfected tagged proteins in HEK293 cells and performed co-immunoprecipitation. We found that TAC-1 co-immunoprecipitated with EFA-6N150, but not with EFA-6N150Δ18 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ZYG-8 and EFA-6N150 could be co-immunoprecipitated when coexpressed.
source: Likewise, ZYG-8 and EFA-6N150 could be co-immunoprecipitated when coexpressed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: After immunoprecipitation of EFA-6N150, both TAC-1 and ZYG-8 could be detected.
source: We further tested binding of EFA-6 to TAC-1 and ZYG-8 in cells co-transfected with EFA-6N150, TAC-1 and ZYG-8ΔKD. After immunoprecipitation of EFA-6N150 we could detect both TAC-1 and ZYG-8, and the interactions between EFA-6 and TAC-1 (or ZYG-8) were not affected by the presence of ZYG-8 (or TAC-1) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The interactions between EFA-6 and TAC-1 were not affected by the presence of ZYG-8.
source: We further tested binding of EFA-6 to TAC-1 and ZYG-8 in cells co-transfected with EFA-6N150, TAC-1 and ZYG-8ΔKD. After immunoprecipitation of EFA-6N150 we could detect both TAC-1 and ZYG-8, and the interactions between EFA-6 and TAC-1 (or ZYG-8) were not affected by the presence of ZYG-8 (or TAC-1) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The interactions between EFA-6 and ZYG-8 were not affected by the presence of TAC-1.
source: We further tested binding of EFA-6 to TAC-1 and ZYG-8 in cells co-transfected with EFA-6N150, TAC-1 and ZYG-8ΔKD. After immunoprecipitation of EFA-6N150 we could detect both TAC-1 and ZYG-8, and the interactions between EFA-6 and TAC-1 (or ZYG-8) were not affected by the presence of ZYG-8 (or TAC-1) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: EFA-6, TAC-1, and ZYG-8 might exist in the same ternary complex.
source: This result suggests that EFA-6, TAC-1, and ZYG-8 might exist in the same ternary complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data showing all three proteins can be detected together.

claim: TAC-1 and ZYG-8 are essential for embryonic cell division.
source: TAC-1 and ZYG-8 are essential for embryonic cell division, and tac-1 and zyg-8 null mutants are maternal-effect embryonic lethal (Gönczy et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gönczy et al., 1999).

claim: tac-1 and zyg-8 null mutants are maternal-effect embryonic lethal.
source: TAC-1 and ZYG-8 are essential for embryonic cell division, and tac-1 and zyg-8 null mutants are maternal-effect embryonic lethal (Gönczy et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gönczy et al., 1999).

claim: zyg-8(lf) mutants displayed normal touch axon morphology when shifted from permissive to restrictive temperature at L1 stage.
source: When shifted from permissive (15°C) to restrictive (25°C) temperature at L1 stage, zyg-8(lf) mutants displayed normal touch axon morphology (not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: zyg-8(lf) mutants showed strongly reduced axon regrowth in both PLM and ALM neurons after axotomy in the L4 stage.
source: After axotomy in the L4 stage, these animals showed strongly reduced axon regrowth in both PLM and ALM neurons, compared to controls subjected to identical temperature shifts (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: zyg-8(lf) mutants showed reduced axon regrowth when maintained at 15°C.
source: zyg-8(lf) mutants also showed reduced axon regrowth when maintained at 15°C, even though PLM axon development was normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D), suggesting that axon regrowth is highly sensitive to reduction of zyg-8 function.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Axon regrowth is highly sensitive to reduction of zyg-8 function.
source: zyg-8(lf) mutants also showed reduced axon regrowth when maintained at 15°C, even though PLM axon development was normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D), suggesting that axon regrowth is highly sensitive to reduction of zyg-8 function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that even at permissive temperature, zyg-8(lf) mutants show reduced regrowth.

claim: The axon regrowth defect in zyg-8(lf) mutants was fully rescued by a single copy transgene expressing ZYG-8 driven by a touch neuron specific promoter.
source: The axon regrowth defect in zyg-8(lf) mutants was fully rescued by a single copy transgene expressing ZYG-8 driven by a touch neuron specific promoter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D), indicating a cell-autonomous function.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: ZYG-8 functions cell-autonomously in axon regrowth.
source: The axon regrowth defect in zyg-8(lf) mutants was fully rescued by a single copy transgene expressing ZYG-8 driven by a touch neuron specific promoter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D), indicating a cell-autonomous function.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell-specific rescue experiment.

claim: tac-1(lf) mutants displayed reduced PLM axon regrowth when shifted from 15 to 25°C in the L1 stage, 20 hr before axotomy.
source: Similarly, tac-1(lf) mutants displayed reduced PLM axon regrowth when shifted from 15 to 25°C in the L1 stage, 20 hr before axotomy (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: In animals with touch neuron specific deletion of tac-1, the PLM axon developed normally, but axon regrowth was impaired.
source: In animals with touch neuron specific deletion of tac-1, the PLM axon developed normally, but axon regrowth was impaired to a degree similar to tac-1(lf) mutants after L1 upshift (Figure 4B), indicating that TAC-1 functions cell autonomously in PLM axon regrowth.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TAC-1 functions cell autonomously in PLM axon regrowth.
source: In animals with touch neuron specific deletion of tac-1, the PLM axon developed normally, but axon regrowth was impaired to a degree similar to tac-1(lf) mutants after L1 upshift (Figure 4B), indicating that TAC-1 functions cell autonomously in PLM axon regrowth.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell-specific deletion experiment.

claim: zyg-8(lf) and tac-1(lf) mutants both displayed significantly reduced regrowth at 6 hpa.
source: zyg-8(lf) and tac-1(lf) mutants both displayed significantly reduced regrowth at 6 hpa, and significantly fewer regenerative growth cones (defined as axonal tips containing filopodia and/or lamellipodia), compared to controls (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: zyg-8(lf) and tac-1(lf) mutants displayed significantly fewer regenerative growth cones at 6 hpa.
source: zyg-8(lf) and tac-1(lf) mutants both displayed significantly reduced regrowth at 6 hpa, and significantly fewer regenerative growth cones (defined as axonal tips containing filopodia and/or lamellipodia), compared to controls (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: tac-1(lf) zyg-8(lf) double mutants did not show further reduction in axon regrowth, compared to single mutants.
source: tac-1(lf) zyg-8(lf) double mutants did not show further reduction in axon regrowth, compared to single mutants (Figure 4A), suggesting TAC-1 and ZYG-8 could act in a common pathway.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TAC-1 and ZYG-8 could act in a common pathway.
source: tac-1(lf) zyg-8(lf) double mutants did not show further reduction in axon regrowth, compared to single mutants (Figure 4A), suggesting TAC-1 and ZYG-8 could act in a common pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effect in the double mutant.

claim: zyg-8(lf) efa-6(0) double mutants resembled zyg-8(lf) single mutants in axon regrowth.
source: zyg-8(lf) efa-6(0) double mutants resembled zyg-8(lf) single mutants, and tac-1(lf) efa-6(0) double mutants resembled tac-1(lf) in axon regrowth (Figure 4A), consistent with zyg-8 and tac-1 acting downstream of efa-6.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: tac-1(lf) efa-6(0) double mutants resembled tac-1(lf) in axon regrowth.
source: zyg-8(lf) efa-6(0) double mutants resembled zyg-8(lf) single mutants, and tac-1(lf) efa-6(0) double mutants resembled tac-1(lf) in axon regrowth (Figure 4A), consistent with zyg-8 and tac-1 acting downstream of efa-6.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: zyg-8 and tac-1 act downstream of efa-6.
source: zyg-8(lf) efa-6(0) double mutants resembled zyg-8(lf) single mutants, and tac-1(lf) efa-6(0) double mutants resembled tac-1(lf) in axon regrowth (Figure 4A), consistent with zyg-8 and tac-1 acting downstream of efa-6.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis analysis.

claim: Overexpression of TAC-1 was sufficient to enhance PLM regrowth.
source: Conversely, overexpression of TAC-1 was sufficient to enhance PLM regrowth, and did not further enhance the regrowth of efa-6(0) mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Overexpression of TAC-1 did not further enhance the regrowth of efa-6(0) mutants.
source: Conversely, overexpression of TAC-1 was sufficient to enhance PLM regrowth, and did not further enhance the regrowth of efa-6(0) mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Loss of EFA-6 function resulted in elevated axonal MT dynamics several hours after injury.
source: Our previous analysis showed that loss of EFA-6 function resulted in elevated axonal MT dynamics several hours after injury (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: In wild type animals, axonal EBP-2::GFP comets were dramatically reduced within 50 s post axotomy.
source: In wild type animals, axonal EBP-2::GFP comets were dramatically reduced within 50 s post axotomy, consistent with injury triggering rapid MT destabilization (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Injury triggers rapid MT destabilization in wild type animals.
source: In wild type animals, axonal EBP-2::GFP comets were dramatically reduced within 50 s post axotomy, consistent with injury triggering rapid MT destabilization (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in EBP-2::GFP comets after injury.

claim: In efa-6(tm3124) or efa-6(ju1200) mutants, there was slightly increased numbers of EBP-2::GFP comets in uninjured axons, compared to wild type.
source: In efa-6(tm3124) or efa-6(ju1200) mutants we observed slightly increased numbers of EBP-2::GFP comets in uninjured axons, compared to wild type; but these animals did not show a significant reduction in EBP-2::GFP comets immediately after injury (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: efa-6(tm3124) or efa-6(ju1200) mutants did not show a significant reduction in EBP-2::GFP comets immediately after injury.
source: In efa-6(tm3124) or efa-6(ju1200) mutants we observed slightly increased numbers of EBP-2::GFP comets in uninjured axons, compared to wild type; but these animals did not show a significant reduction in EBP-2::GFP comets immediately after injury (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In efa-6(gf) animals overexpressing EFA-6N150, the total number of growing MT plus ends in uninjured axons was reduced compared to wild type.
source: In efa-6(gf) animals overexpressing EFA-6N150, the total number of growing MT plus ends in uninjured axons was reduced compared to wild type, and was not further reduced after injury (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In efa-6(gf) animals overexpressing EFA-6N150, the number of growing MT plus ends was not further reduced after injury.
source: In efa-6(gf) animals overexpressing EFA-6N150, the total number of growing MT plus ends in uninjured axons was reduced compared to wild type, and was not further reduced after injury (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: tac-1(lf) mutants had slightly reduced axonal MT dynamics in uninjured axons.
source: tac-1(lf) mutants had slightly reduced axonal MT dynamics in uninjured axons, and displayed injury-dependent downregulation, whereas zyg-8(lf) mutants showed fewer dynamic MTs in uninjured axons, and did not further downregulate MTs after injury (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: tac-1(lf) mutants displayed injury-dependent downregulation of MT dynamics.
source: tac-1(lf) mutants had slightly reduced axonal MT dynamics in uninjured axons, and displayed injury-dependent downregulation, whereas zyg-8(lf) mutants showed fewer dynamic MTs in uninjured axons, and did not further downregulate MTs after injury (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: zyg-8(lf) mutants showed fewer dynamic MTs in uninjured axons.
source: tac-1(lf) mutants had slightly reduced axonal MT dynamics in uninjured axons, and displayed injury-dependent downregulation, whereas zyg-8(lf) mutants showed fewer dynamic MTs in uninjured axons, and did not further downregulate MTs after injury (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: zyg-8(lf) mutants did not further downregulate MTs after injury.
source: tac-1(lf) mutants had slightly reduced axonal MT dynamics in uninjured axons, and displayed injury-dependent downregulation, whereas zyg-8(lf) mutants showed fewer dynamic MTs in uninjured axons, and did not further downregulate MTs after injury (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: tac-1(0) touch neurons displayed reduced dynamics in uninjured axons similar to zyg-8(lf).
source: We further tested the tac-1(ok3305) deletion allele using Cre-induced tissue-specific knockout ('Materials and methods'). Compared to control, tac-1(0) touch neurons displayed reduced dynamics in uninjured axons similar to zyg-8(lf), and showed no further reduction after injury (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: tac-1(0) touch neurons showed no further reduction in MT dynamics after injury.
source: We further tested the tac-1(ok3305) deletion allele using Cre-induced tissue-specific knockout ('Materials and methods'). Compared to control, tac-1(0) touch neurons displayed reduced dynamics in uninjured axons similar to zyg-8(lf), and showed no further reduction after injury (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Dynamic axonal MTs are significantly increased at 3 hr post axotomy.
source: As reported previously, dynamic axonal MTs are significantly increased at 3 hr post axotomy, and this is further enhanced in efa-6(0) mutants (Chen et al., 2011) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: The increase in dynamic axonal MTs at 3 hr post axotomy is further enhanced in efa-6(0) mutants.
source: As reported previously, dynamic axonal MTs are significantly increased at 3 hr post axotomy, and this is further enhanced in efa-6(0) mutants (Chen et al., 2011) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2011).

claim: Neither tac-1(lf) nor zyg-8(lf) mutants upregulated dynamic axonal MTs by 3 hr post injury.
source: Neither tac-1(lf) nor zyg-8(lf) mutants upregulated dynamic axonal MTs by 3 hr post injury (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MT dynamics in efa-6(0) tac-1(lf) or efa-6(0) zyg-8(lf) double mutants resembled tac-1(lf) or zyg-8(lf) single mutants.
source: Moreover, MT dynamics in efa-6(0) tac-1(lf) or efa-6(0) zyg-8(lf) double mutants resembled tac-1(lf) or zyg-8(lf) single mutants (Figure 5B), consistent with EFA-6 functioning upstream of ZYG-8.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: EFA-6 functions upstream of ZYG-8.
source: Moreover, MT dynamics in efa-6(0) tac-1(lf) or efa-6(0) zyg-8(lf) double mutants resembled tac-1(lf) or zyg-8(lf) single mutants (Figure 5B), consistent with EFA-6 functioning upstream of ZYG-8.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis analysis.

claim: Axon injury causes an immediate inhibition in growing MTs, dependent on EFA-6.
source: Thus, axon injury causes an immediate inhibition in growing MTs, dependent on EFA-6 and correlating with its relocalization, followed by a more prolonged increase in growing MTs, dependent on the function of TAC-1 and ZYG-8.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the MT dynamics experiments.

claim: The immediate inhibition in growing MTs after injury correlates with EFA-6 relocalization.
source: Thus, axon injury causes an immediate inhibition in growing MTs, dependent on EFA-6 and correlating with its relocalization, followed by a more prolonged increase in growing MTs, dependent on the function of TAC-1 and ZYG-8.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal correlation between EFA-6 relocalization and MT dynamics changes.

claim: After injury, there is a more prolonged increase in growing MTs, dependent on the function of TAC-1 and ZYG-8.
source: Thus, axon injury causes an immediate inhibition in growing MTs, dependent on EFA-6 and correlating with its relocalization, followed by a more prolonged increase in growing MTs, dependent on the function of TAC-1 and ZYG-8.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the MT dynamics experiments.

claim: In wild type uninjured touch neurons, GFP::ZYG-8 was diffuse throughout axon.
source: In wild type uninjured touch neurons, GFP::ZYG-8 was diffuse throughout axon (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GFP::TAC-1 localized to one or two perinuclear spots in the soma and was also diffusely distributed along the axon.
source: GFP::TAC-1 or TAC-1::GFP localized to one or two perinuclear spots in the soma and was also diffusely distributed along the axon (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The localization patterns of GFP::ZYG-8 and GFP::TAC-1 were not altered in efa-6(0).
source: These patterns were not altered in efa-6(0) (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Steady state localization of GFP::EFA-6FL or GFP::EFA-6N150 was normal in tac-1(0) or zyg-8(0).
source: Conversely, steady state localization of GFP::EFA-6FL or GFP::EFA-6N150 was normal in tac-1(0) or zyg-8(0) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In uninjured axons, EFA-6, TAC-1, and ZYG-8 appear to localize independently.
source: Thus, in uninjured axons, EFA-6, TAC-1, and ZYG-8 appear to localize independently.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of one protein does not affect the localization of the others.

claim: GFP::ZYG-8 localization is not affected by axon injury.
source: Whereas GFP::ZYG-8 remained diffuse after injury (Figure 6A), TAC-1::GFP or GFP::TAC-1 relocalized rapidly to puncta along the axon and in the soma (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TAC-1::GFP or GFP::TAC-1 relocalized rapidly to puncta along the axon and in the soma after injury.
source: Whereas GFP::ZYG-8 remained diffuse after injury (Figure 6A), TAC-1::GFP or GFP::TAC-1 relocalized rapidly to puncta along the axon and in the soma (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The large perinuclear TAC-1 spots recruited EFA-6.
source: We next co-expressed EFA-6FL::GFP and mKate2::TAC-1 in touch neurons, and found that while EFA-6FL::GFP localized to the plasma membrane throughout the cell, the large perinuclear TAC-1 spots also recruited EFA-6 (Figure 6D), suggesting the two proteins can interact in neurons.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization imaging data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: EFA-6 and TAC-1 can interact in neurons.
source: We next co-expressed EFA-6FL::GFP and mKate2::TAC-1 in touch neurons, and found that while EFA-6FL::GFP localized to the plasma membrane throughout the cell, the large perinuclear TAC-1 spots also recruited EFA-6 (Figure 6D), suggesting the two proteins can interact in neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization of EFA-6 and TAC-1 at perinuclear spots.

claim: After injury axonal EFA-6FL::GFP and mKate2::TAC-1 relocalized to largely overlapping puncta.
source: After injury axonal EFA-6FL::GFP and mKate2::TAC-1 relocalized to largely overlapping puncta (Figure 6D); co-expressed EFA-6N150::mKate2 and TAC-1::GFP displayed similar co-localization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization imaging data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The injury-induced re-localization of GFP::TAC-1 occurred normally in efa-6(ju1200).
source: The injury-induced re-localization of GFP::TAC-1 occurred normally in efa-6(ju1200) (Figure 6B), as did re-localization of GFP::EFA-6N150 in tac-1(0) or zyg-8(0) (Figure 6C), suggesting that these proteins relocalize independently of each other.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Re-localization of GFP::EFA-6N150 occurred normally in tac-1(0) or zyg-8(0).
source: The injury-induced re-localization of GFP::TAC-1 occurred normally in efa-6(ju1200) (Figure 6B), as did re-localization of GFP::EFA-6N150 in tac-1(0) or zyg-8(0) (Figure 6C), suggesting that these proteins relocalize independently of each other.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: EFA-6, TAC-1, and ZYG-8 relocalize independently of each other after injury.
source: The injury-induced re-localization of GFP::TAC-1 occurred normally in efa-6(ju1200) (Figure 6B), as did re-localization of GFP::EFA-6N150 in tac-1(0) or zyg-8(0) (Figure 6C), suggesting that these proteins relocalize independently of each other.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of one protein does not affect the relocalization of the others.

claim: PTRN-1 is the C. elegans member of the Patronin/CAMSAP family.
source: PTRN-1 is the C. elegans member of the Patronin/CAMSAP family, known to bind to and stabilize MT minus ends (Meng et al., 2008; Goodwin and Vale, 2010; Yau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Meng et al., 2008; Goodwin and Vale, 2010; Yau et al., 2014).

claim: PTRN-1 is known to bind to and stabilize MT minus ends.
source: PTRN-1 is the C. elegans member of the Patronin/CAMSAP family, known to bind to and stabilize MT minus ends (Meng et al., 2008; Goodwin and Vale, 2010; Yau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Meng et al., 2008; Goodwin and Vale, 2010; Yau et al., 2014).

claim: In C. elegans neurons PTRN-1 localizes to axonal puncta, likely the sites of MT minus ends.
source: In C. elegans neurons PTRN-1 localizes to axonal puncta, likely the sites of MT minus ends (Chuang et al., 2014; Marcette et al., 2014; Richardson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Chuang et al., 2014; Marcette et al., 2014; Richardson et al., 2014).

claim: GFP::PTRN-1 localization does not dramatically change after axon injury.
source: GFP::PTRN-1 localization does not dramatically change after axon injury (Chuang et al., 2014), while in the same time period EFA-6N150::mKate2 became punctate and partially colocalized with GFP::PTRN-1, independent of the tagged reporters (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Chuang et al., 2014).

claim: After injury, EFA-6N150::mKate2 became punctate and partially colocalized with GFP::PTRN-1.
source: GFP::PTRN-1 localization does not dramatically change after axon injury (Chuang et al., 2014), while in the same time period EFA-6N150::mKate2 became punctate and partially colocalized with GFP::PTRN-1, independent of the tagged reporters (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization imaging data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: After injury, TAC-1::mKate2 became highly colocalized with GFP::PTRN-1.
source: Similarly, after injury TAC-1::mKate2 became highly colocalized with GFP::PTRN-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Axon injury causes TAC-1 to relocalize to PTRN-1-containing puncta.
source: These observations suggest that axon injury causes TAC-1 to relocalize to PTRN-1-containing puncta, and causes EFA-6 to relocalize to regions overlapping with or closely adjacent to the TAC-1/PTRN-1 puncta.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data.

claim: Axon injury causes EFA-6 to relocalize to regions overlapping with or closely adjacent to the TAC-1/PTRN-1 puncta.
